conceptTag: Ford's Model T and the moving assembly line
readerTitle: The Model T got cheaper every year. Then it stopped selling.
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Ford Model T, General Motors) + 가상 적용 (급여 관리 소프트웨어)
insight: 규모의 경제는 공짜가 아니다. 단위당 원가를 낮추는 거대한 고정 투자는 제품을 '똑같이' 만드는 데서 나오고, 고객이 원하는 것이 바뀌면 그 투자가 족쇄가 된다.
misconception: 단위당 원가를 가장 낮게 만드는 회사가 결국 시장을 이긴다.

sources.text: Ford Motor Company, corporate history: Model T (1908) and the moving assembly line at Highland Park (1913)
The Henry Ford (museum), Model T and assembly line history resources
Henry Ford with Samuel Crowther, My Life and Work (1922), the 'any color so long as it is black' line
Alfred P. Sloan Jr., My Years with General Motors (1964), GM's product range, annual model changes and the 1920s competition with Ford
David A. Hounshell, From the American System to Mass Production, 1800–1932 (1984), assembly times, the Model T's decline and the Model A changeover

factChecks.note: 1908년 Model T 투어링카 가격 $850, 1920년대 중반 기본 모델 $300 미만(Ford 자료에는 1925년 $260 등으로 나옴)은 Ford 공식 역사와 The Henry Ford 자료로 확인하세요. 카드에는 '$850 → under $300'로만 적었습니다.
섀시 조립 시간 '12시간 이상 → 약 1.5시간(93분)'은 Ford 공식 역사와 Hounshell(1984)에 나오는 수치입니다. 자료마다 분 단위가 조금씩 다르므로 '12+ hours', '~1.5 hours'로 적었습니다.
1927년까지 1,500만 대 이상 생산, 마지막 Model T 생산 1927년 5월, Model A로 전환하며 공장이 수개월 멈춘 점(Model A는 1927년 말 출시)을 Ford 공식 역사로 확인하세요.
'1927년 Chevrolet가 Ford 판매량을 앞섰다'는 Sloan(1964)과 Hounshell(1984) 등에서 확인하세요.
검정색 인용문은 My Life and Work(1922)에 나오는 문장을 줄여 인용했습니다. 원문: 'Any customer can have a car painted any colour that he wants so long as it is black.' 공저자(Samuel Crowther)가 있다는 점도 참고하세요.
GM 브랜드들이 부품을 공유했다는 내용과 Model A가 잘 팔렸다는 내용은 일반적인 수준으로만 적었습니다. 구체적인 수치는 넣지 않았습니다. Sloan(1964)과 Hounshell(1984)로 확인하세요.

cards.title: The Model T got cheaper every year. Then it stopped selling.
body: In 1908, a Ford Model T touring car cost $850. By the mid-1920s, a basic Model T sold for under $300, and Ford had built more than 15 million of them.
Then, in 1927, Ford stopped making it and shut its factories for months. The thing that made the car so cheap also made it hard to change.

image.label: Rows of identical black early cars on a factory floor
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 1910~20년대풍의 똑같은 검은색 자동차 수십 대가 공장 바닥에 줄지어 있고, 한쪽 구석에 색깔 있는 신형 차 한 대가 서 있음. 실제 Ford·GM 로고나 엠블럼은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Demand is outrunning your factory.
body: It's around 1912. You make one car, and it sells faster than your workers can build it. Teams still assemble each car by walking around a frame that stays in one place.

options.text: Raise the price. Demand is clearly higher than supply
options.feedback: You'd earn more per car right away. But the market stays small, mostly people who could already afford a car.

options.text: Add more models to reach more kinds of buyers
options.feedback: More buyers, yes. But every new model needs its own parts, tools and training, so your cost per car stays high.

options.text: Spend heavily on machines and a new line built for this one car, then cut the price
options.feedback: Roughly what Ford did. It's a huge up-front cost that only pays off if you sell a lot of identical cars. Keep that *if* in mind.

cards.title: Move the car, not the workers.

breakdown.label: Chassis assembly before
breakdown.detail: Teams built each car in one spot

cards.callout: In 1913, at its Highland Park plant, Ford began pulling cars past workers. Each worker repeated one small task, again and again.

cards.title: Economies of scale
body: **Economies of scale** means your cost per unit falls as you make more.

Ford's moving line and special machines cost a fortune up front. That's a fixed cost: it stays the same whether you build ten thousand cars or a million. Spread over millions of identical cars, it shrinks to a small amount per car.
Lower costs let Ford cut prices. Lower prices sold more cars. More cars spread the fixed cost even thinner.

image.label: Loop: big investment, more cars, lower cost, lower price
image.brief: 순환 화살표 인포그래픽. "Big fixed investment" → "Cost per car falls" → "Lower price" → "More cars sold" → 다시 "Cost per car falls". 한쪽에 큰 기계 덩어리가 작은 조각들로 나뉘어 차 위에 하나씩 올라가는 그림.

cards.title: Then the buyers changed.
body: By the mid-1920s, many families already owned a car. The next buyer wanted something better, not just something cheap.
General Motors, led by Alfred Sloan, offered a range of brands from Chevrolet up to Cadillac. It added new styling every year, colors and buying on credit. The Model T barely changed.
In 1927, Chevrolet outsold Ford. Ford ended the Model T that May and closed its plants for months to retool for the new Model A.

image.label: One unchanged black car beside a lineup of varied colorful cars
image.brief: 왼쪽에 똑같은 검은 차 한 대, 오른쪽에 색과 크기가 다른 차 다섯 대가 계단식으로 늘어선 그림(저가→고가). 실제 브랜드 로고와 엠블럼은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: The machines only knew one car.
body: Ford's low cost came from doing one thing the same way, millions of times. Machines and tools built for one car couldn't simply make a different one. Changing the product meant rebuilding much of the investment.
In his 1922 memoir, Ford wrote that a customer could have any color he wanted *so long as it is black*. That sameness wasn't a side effect. **It was the cost model.**

cards.title: Scale didn't fail. Rigid scale did.
body: GM used scale too. Its brands could share many parts behind different looks, so it got low costs and variety at the same time. Ford recovered as well: the Model A sold well.

The lesson isn't to avoid big investments. Scale pays best when customers want the same thing for a long time. When their wants are shifting, keep some flexibility, even if each unit costs a bit more.

cards.title: Now it's payroll software.
body: Your payroll app serves small restaurants. Every customer gets the same product, so serving one more costs you almost nothing.
Now retail chains are asking for it, but they need different shift rules and reports. What do you do?

options.text: Keep one product and say no to every change
options.feedback: Your cost per customer stays lowest. But if the market moves toward needs like these, you risk becoming the Model T.

options.text: Build a custom version for each big chain
options.feedback: You win the deals, but each version needs its own code, testing and support. Your cost advantage quietly disappears.

options.text: Keep one shared core and add settings customers can switch on
options.feedback: Like GM's shared parts: most of the cost stays spread across everyone, and customers still get variety. Building the settings costs more up front.

cards.title: Scale makes each unit cheaper by making every unit the same.
body: That's a great deal while customers want the same thing. It turns into a trap when they stop.
**Try it today:** list your two or three biggest fixed investments. For each, ask: if customers wanted something different next year, could it adapt?
